profile.feeling: A tomato stew of okra and lamb with rice — home cooking from Egypt to Iraq; people love or hate its slime.

senses.def: okra, ladies’ fingers — the pods, and the stew made with them (mass noun)

examples.tr: My mother cooks okra with meat and tomatoes.
I choose small okra because it is more tender.

examples.text: يُقَدَّمُ مَرَقُ الْبَامِيَةِ مَعَ الْأَرُزِّ فِي الْعِرَاقِ.
examples.tr: In Iraq okra stew is served with rice.
I bought frozen okra.

synonyms.nuance: spelling of the pronunciation bāmya (Wiktionary translation tables)

etymology.text: Origin unknown (Wiktionary). One suggestion: a dialectal form of إِبْهَام (“thumb”) + the dish suffix ـِيَّة — the pods look like fingers, as in English “ladies’ fingers”.

funFacts: Turkish bamya and Greek μπάμια (bámia) come from this Arabic word.
pitfalls: In Morocco okra is called مْلُوخِيَّة — elsewhere that word is jute mallow (Wiktionary).
Feminine: الْبَامِيَةُ طَازَجَةٌ (the okra is fresh).
subtleties: A mass noun: one pod is حَبَّةُ بَامِيَةٍ.

profile.feeling: The breakfast of Egypt: slow-cooked ful with oil, cumin and bread — and fresh green pods in spring.

senses.def: broad beans, fava beans (Vicia faba; collective, one bean = فُولَة)
the dish of stewed dried fava beans (فُولٌ مُدَمَّسٌ, ful medames)

examples.tr: I shelled the green broad beans for cooking.
My father bought a kilo of green broad beans.

examples.text: تُصْنَعُ الطَّعْمِيَّةُ فِي مِصْرَ مِنَ الْفُولِ.
examples.tr: In Egypt, taʿmiyya (falafel) is made from fava beans.
We eat ful medames for breakfast.

phrases.tr: like a fava bean split in two (Egyptian Arabic)
phrases.meaning: as alike as two peas in a pod (of two people who look the same)

synonyms.nuance: the classical word (also بَاقِلَاء), feminine and diptote; everyday in Iraq and the Gulf as باجلا (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: Claimed to be borrowed from Aramaic pōlā (“bean”), perhaps ultimately from Proto-Semitic *pūl- (Wiktionary); compare Hebrew פּוֹל (pol, broad bean).

funFacts: Egyptian falafel (طَعْمِيَّة) is made from fava beans, not from chickpeas as in the Levant.
Hebrew פּוֹל (pol) is the same word.
pitfalls: فُولٌ سُودَانِيٌّ is peanuts, not a kind of fava bean.
Collective: الْفُولُ = the beans in general; فُولَة = one bean; فُولَات = beans counted (Wiktionary also gives the plural أَفْوَال).
subtleties: فُول is both the raw legume and the famous cooked dish; فُولٌ مُدَمَّسٌ is the slow-simmered dried beans.

profile.feeling: A word from the Prophet’s table: the gourd he loved, famous from the ḥadīth.

senses.def: gourd, especially the bottle gourd, calabash (Lagenaria siceraria) (collective; one gourd = دُبَّاءَة)

examples.tr: The Prophet used to love gourd.
We cooked the gourd with meat.

examples.text: صُنِعَ هٰذَا الْإِنَاءُ مِنْ دُبَّاءَةٍ مُجَفَّفَةٍ.
examples.tr: This vessel was made from a dried gourd.

synonyms.nuance: the everyday word for pumpkins, squashes and gourds; it covers the bottle gourd too
the Qurʾānic word (37:146) for the gourd plant that shaded Jonah, which commentators identify with الدُّبَّاء

etymology.text: From دَبَّ (dabba, “to crawl”) — the creeping vine (Wiktionary).

funFacts: The Companion Anas ibn Mālik reported that after seeing the Prophet pick out the pieces of gourd from a dish, he himself always loved gourd (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī).
Dried gourds served as vessels: a ḥadīth forbids making nabīdh in الدُّبَّاء and some other kinds of vessel.
pitfalls: Unlike هِنْدِبَاءُ (a diptote), دُبَّاء takes tanwīn: دُبَّاءٌ, accusative دُبَّاءً (Wiktionary).
Classical and religious register: in today’s kitchens people mostly say قَرْع.
subtleties: Collective: الدُّبَّاءُ (gourd as food), دُبَّاءَة (one gourd), دُبَّاءَات (gourds counted).

profile.feeling: A spring delicacy: hearts stuffed, or stewed with peas and dill — some work to clean.

examples.tr: I cleaned the artichokes and kept only the hearts.
I bought fresh artichokes at the market.
Stuffed artichoke hearts are a spring dish.

synonyms.nuance: Levantine name, refitted from English “artichoke” to native words meaning “earthy-thorny” (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: Perhaps connected to Akkadian arsuppu (a cereal or produce with a scaly look), or from Middle Persian *xār-čōp, “thorn stick” (Wiktionary).

funFacts: English artichoke, Italian carciofo and Spanish alcachofa all come from Andalusian Arabic al-ḵaršūfa.
Modern Hebrew חֻרְשָׁף (ḥurshaf) is the same word.
pitfalls: The plural خَرَاشِيف is a diptote: خَرَاشِيفُ, accusative and genitive خَرَاشِيفَ — no tanwīn (Wiktionary).
Not the Jerusalem artichoke, which is a tuber of the sunflower family.
subtleties: An ordinary countable noun in Wiktionary (خُرْشُوفٌ, plural خَرَاشِيفُ); Egyptian Arabic says ḵaršūf, with a unit noun ḵaršūfa (Wiktionary).
Levantine أَرْضِي شَوْكِي is a phono-semantic match of English “artichoke”: “earthy-thorny” (Wiktionary).

profile.feeling: The bath-house sponge more than a food: a dried luffa scrubs your back.

senses.def: luffa, sponge gourd (Luffa) — the plant and its fruit (collective; one gourd = لُوفَة)
a bath sponge made from the dried fruit
arum (Arum spp., Arisarum vulgare), a wild plant (Wiktionary)

examples.text: تُؤْكَلُ ثِمَارُ اللُّوفِ الصَّغِيرَةُ فِي آسِيَا.
examples.tr: The young luffa fruits are eaten in Asia.
My neighbour grew luffa on the fence.
I used a luffa (sponge) in the bath.

synonyms.nuance: the MSA word for fibre and for the sponge; one sponge = لِيفَة (Wiktionary)

etymology.text: Variant of لِيف (līf, “fibre”), more dialectal outside the botanical senses (Wiktionary).

funFacts: English loofah and the botanical name Luffa come from this Arabic word.
pitfalls: Wiktionary also gives لُوف for arum, a wild plant — context decides.
In everyday MSA the sponge is mostly لِيفَة (from لِيف, fibre).
subtleties: Collective: اللُّوفُ (the plant, the gourds), لُوفَة (one gourd or one sponge), لُوفَات (counted).

ref.src: Wiktionary (kaikki.org): translation table of English kale; كرنب, أجعد

profile.feeling: A new “superfood” on supermarket shelves: dark, crinkly leaves.

examples.text: أَضَفْتُ الْكُرُنْبَ الْأَجْعَدَ إِلَى الْعَصِيرِ الْأَخْضَرِ.
examples.tr: I added kale to the green juice.
Kale leaves are a little tough.

examples.text: يُبَاعُ الْكُرُنْبُ الْأَجْعَدُ فِي الْمَتَاجِرِ الْكَبِيرَةِ.
examples.tr: Kale is sold in the big stores.

profile.synonymsNone: No established single word: kale is new in Arab markets; the English name is often just transliterated.

etymology.text: كُرُنْب “cabbage, kale”, borrowed from Ancient Greek κράμβη + أَجْعَد “creased, frizzled”, a colour-or-defect adjective from the root ج ع د (Wiktionary).
etymology.src: Wiktionary (kaikki.org): كرنب, أجعد and the translation table of English kale

funFacts: كُرُنْب is Greek κράμβη; German Grünkohl, “green cabbage”, looks at the same plant from another angle.
pitfalls: أَجْعَد is a diptote: كُرُنْبٌ أَجْعَدُ, genitive كُرُنْبٍ أَجْعَدَ.
Wiktionary’s translation is vocalized كُرْنُب (kurnub); its entry has كُرُنْب (kurunb), used here.
subtleties: شَعْرٌ أَجْعَدُ = curly hair: the same adjective.

ref.src: Wiktionary (kaikki.org): ملفوف; the phrase has no entry

profile.feeling: A purple crunch in salads — and a little chemistry show in the pot.

examples.tr: I like red cabbage salad with lemon.
I cut the red cabbage into thin strips.

examples.text: يَتَغَيَّرُ لَوْنُ الْمَلْفُوفِ الْأَحْمَرِ مَعَ الْخَلِّ.
examples.tr: The colour of red cabbage changes with vinegar.
I bought a head of red cabbage.

synonyms.nuance: with the Egyptian and classical word for cabbage

etymology.text: مَلْفُوف “cabbage”, literally “the wrapped one”, the passive participle of لَفَّ (Wiktionary) + أَحْمَر “red”.
etymology.src: Wiktionary (kaikki.org): ملفوف; the phrase has no entry

funFacts: Red cabbage juice is a natural pH indicator: it turns red with acid and blue-green with alkali.
German says Rotkohl or, in the south, Blaukraut — red or blue, depending on the region (and the cook’s vinegar).
pitfalls: The adjective is a diptote: مَلْفُوفٌ أَحْمَرُ, genitive مَلْفُوفٍ أَحْمَرَ.
subtleties: Masculine agreement, because مَلْفُوف is masculine: الْمَلْفُوفُ الْأَحْمَرُ طَازَجٌ.

absent.reason: Not part of most Arab cuisines; no established everyday word. Wiktionary lists قَاوُون, which otherwise means melon (from Turkish kavun), so it is ambiguous.
absent.use: descriptive names such as قَرْعٌ مُرٌّ (“bitter gourd”)

No word of its own: collards are not distinguished from other leafy cabbages.
